parole.significato: nominative singular ending of most strong masculine nouns
parole.testo: From Old Norse -r (nominative singular ending for i-, u-, masculine a-stems, and masculine consonant stem nouns, as well as most masculine adjectives). In turn, the Old Norse endings all stem from Proto-Indo-European *-s, a general-purpose masculine/feminine singular nominative ending.
From Old Norse barki, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“to bore, pierce”), akin to Armenian բերան (beran, “mouth”).
From Old Norse belja (“bellow, roar”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to roar”), of onomatopoeic origin. Compare German bellen, English bellow, Luxembourgish billen.

From Old Norse brattr, brantr, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰren- (“project”), related to Old English brant (“steep”), Latvian bruôds (“roof ridge”). Cognate with Faroese brattur, Norwegian Bokmål bratt, Danish brat, Swedish brant, and Old English brant, bront (Englis
From Old Norse ekla (“scarcity”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eg- (“to lack”).
From Old Norse elgiar, according to Pokorny, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elgʰ- (“cold, frost”), see also Latin algidus, Albanian alkë (“white”).

From Old Norse fálma, perhaps imitative of fumbling. Or, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to shake, swing”), see also Latin palpō (“to pat, touch softly”), and possibly Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan (“to feel”).
From Old Norse gaula (“to howl”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂w- (“to gape, yawn”), related to Lithuanian gomurys (“palate”).
From Old Norse gusa (“to spurt”), from Proto-Indo-European *gus-, from *ǵʰew- (“to pour”). Related to Icelandic gjósa, geysa, English gush and geyser.

From Old Norse hlíta (“to rely on, trust, abide by”), according to Pokorny, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean, incline”). Cognate with Swedish lita (“to trust, rely on, depend on, confide in”), Danish lide (“to trust”), and English lite (“to expect, wait”).

parole.significato: to ruminate, to chew the cud
parole.testo: From Old Norse jórtra, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewg- (“to roar, belch”), see also Old English rocettan (“to burp”).

parole.significato: to dive, to go so deep underwater that one can't be seen
parole.testo: From Old Norse kafa (cognate with Faroese kava), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷebʰ- (“to dive, dive in”). Possibly cognate with Ancient Greek βάπτω (báptō).

From Old Norse lýja, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to cut off, to separate”). Possible cognates include English loose, Latin luō (“to expiate, to pay”), Ancient Greek λῡ́ω (lū́ō, “to loosen”).
From Old Norse miðr, from earlier minnr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“little, small”), cognate with Gothic 𐌼𐌹𐌽𐍃 (mins), Latin minus.
From Old Norse myki (“dung”), from Proto-Indo-European *mewg- (“slick, slimy”). Cognates include Middle English mok and muk (English muck).
From Old Norse skrafa, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krep-.

From Old Norse skreppa (“small bag”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerbʰ- (“to turn (around), wind”), see also Latin corbis (“basket”), Ancient Greek κάρφος (kárphos, “dry stalk”), German Scherbe (“fragment”).
From Old Norse ótti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʰ- (“to fear, to be afraid”). Related to aga, agi.
From Old Norse úr, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wers- (“to rain”), in which case related to Latin urina.
